analysis.subject: earth-science
analysis.pageCoverage: Page explains earthquake magnitude types and logarithmic scales, how energy release relates to magnitude, and how shaking intensity varies with distance, depth and local geology, using examples from California and Washington earthquakes.

overview.headline: How magnitude, energy release and shaking intensity are measured and related

keyPoints.point: Students understand that magnitude is a single value describing earthquake size while intensity varies by location.
keyPoints.quote: Whereas the magnitude of an earthquake is one value that describes the size

keyPoints.point: Students understand that each whole number increase in magnitude represents a tenfold increase in measured amplitude on a seismogram.
keyPoints.quote: each whole number increase in magnitude represents a tenfold increase in measured amplitude as measured on a seismogram.

keyPoints.point: Students understand that a whole number increase in magnitude corresponds to about 32 times more energy release.
keyPoints.quote: While each whole number increase in magnitude represents a tenfold increase in the measured amplitude, it represents an 32 times more energy release.

keyPoints.point: Students understand that seismic moment is calculated from rigidity, area and slip on the fault.
keyPoints.quote: Moment (MO) = rigidity x area x slip

keyTerms.gloss: single number describing the size of an earthquake
keyTerms.quote: Magnitude is the size of the earthquake.

keyTerms.gloss: measure of shaking at a place that varies with distance and local geology
keyTerms.quote: The intensity is the measure of shaking at each location

keyTerms.gloss: sensitive instrument that provides the recorded vibrations that travel through earth
keyTerms.quote: The time, location, and magnitude of an earthquake can be determined from the data recorded by seismometer.

keyTerms.gloss: strength of rock along the fault that resists slip
keyTerms.quote: where rigidity is the strength of the rock along the fault, area is the area of the fault that slipped, and slip is the distance the fault moved.

keyTerms.gloss: scale used in the United States to express intensity in roman numerals
keyTerms.quote: The intensity scale that we use in the United States is called the Modified Mercalli Intensity Scale, but other countries use other scales.

componentPlan.pedagogicalReason: Logarithmic scaling is central to magnitude and energy, students need to visualise tenfold amplitude and large energy jumps.
componentPlan.focusQuote: each whole number increase in magnitude represents a tenfold increase in measured amplitude as measured on a seismogram.

componentPlan.pedagogicalReason: The moment magnitude formula links physical fault properties to the magnitude number students see in reports.
